synopsis.statement: swe-prep is a single-user, habit-forming interview-prep app that runs your code: the daily loop is a ~4-minute warm-up of ~8 quick reps that alone completes the day, an optional ~30-minute main exercise, and open-ended continuation after that. It is Spring Boot 3.4.x on Java 21 with Postgres, a React + Vite front end, and the Monaco editor, run locally and reached over a tailnet; the engine is public while all problem content lives in the separate private swe-prep-content repo, loaded from a gitignored local clone.

nodes.title: Public engine, private problem content
nodes.question: Can Blind 75 problem statements ship in a public repository, and if not, what is the cheapest lawful source of problem text?
nodes.decision: Ship the engine publicly and keep all problem content - statements, test data, reference solutions, generators - in the private repo the solutions already go to, loaded by the app via a private submodule or a gitignored local path. The public repo keeps the engine, the list of problem titles, and optionally a few original demo statements.
nodes.why: LeetCode's statement prose, worked examples and constraint framing are copyrighted expression, while the list of problems, titles and underlying algorithmic ideas are free facts (17 U.S.C. §102(b)). The streak decision had already sent solutions to a separate private repo, so three of the authoring unit's four parts (statement, test cases, reference solution, input generator) were going private anyway; moving the statement across costs nothing and leaves the public, portfolio-facing repo with zero protected prose. It is also the fastest path to the first daily session, the map's binding constraint, since no 75-statement authoring project stands in the way.

rejected.alternative: Using an openly-licensed collection of Blind 75 / NeetCode 150 statements
rejected.why_it_lost: None exists and none can: Blind 75 is a curated list of LeetCode's problems, and repos claiming to have it either license only their author's solution code (e.g. kamyu104/LeetCode-Solutions, MIT over the code, not the prose) or reproduce LeetCode text with no right to grant.

rejected.alternative: Adopting clean, genuinely reusable datasets (HumanEval, MBPP, Exercism problem-specifications)
rejected.why_it_lost: They are general or entry-level programming katas rather than interview-algorithm curation, so adopting them would mean abandoning the curated set - useful as a format demo, not as the content pile.

rejected.alternative: Using scraped aggregate datasets with permissive wrapper licences (APPS, CodeContests)
rejected.why_it_lost: A permissive wrapper licence does not cure scraped provenance: their problems are collected from Codeforces, Kattis, AtCoder and others, and a licensor can only license what they own.

rejected.alternative: Writing fresh original statements now, as a gate before drilling
rejected.why_it_lost: Confirmed clean because the algorithm is unprotectable, but it loses as a gate purely on time; it is good later work for portfolio polish.

rejected.alternative: Scraping Blind 75 statements into the app
rejected.why_it_lost: LeetCode's ToS forbids crawling, scraping and spidering outright, independent of the copyright analysis and regardless of whether content lands in a public or private repo, so it is off the table permanently.

nodes.soundbite: The problem statements go into the private repo with the solutions, and the public repo ships the engine and the list of titles.

nodes.title: Submission judging model
nodes.question: How a submission is judged when the captain hits run: pass/fail or partial credit, whether time and memory limits are graded or reported, whether the app comments on approach or only correctness, what feedback appears on failure, and whether a submission's result is durable.
nodes.decision: Correctness is strict pass/fail with no partial credit, showing the count of tests passed as information rather than a score. On failure the app reports only how many tests failed; an explicit request reveals input, expected, and actual, and using it is recorded visibly but never penalised, matching the hint ladder's shape of help that is always available, always chosen, always recorded. Each problem carries an authored target complexity; after tests pass the user states their solution's time and space complexity before the target is revealed, and the claim is verified by running the submission at growing input sizes and fitting the runtime curve, with only coarse claims made and inconclusive measurement reported as 'measured scaling is consistent with your claim'. Style feedback is none. Resource limits are reported, not graded, with a generous timeout to catch infinite loops. Every attempt is persisted with pass/fail, submissions taken, hint-ladder rungs climbed, whether the failing case was revealed, the complexity self-assessment and what measurement said about it, and whether the exercise was abandoned.
nodes.why: Partial credit would invent a number that means nothing and soften the only honest signal available. Reasoning about your own code without an oracle is the skill a real interview tests, and always handing over the failing case trains the opposite reflex; penalties on a self-imposed system only teach the user to game themselves. Correctness is the floor, not the bar, and articulating complexity out loud is itself the interview skill, but a self-report alone would congratulate an O(n^2) solution claiming O(n), so it is scored against empirical measurement, which reliably catches polynomial blow-up though it cannot separate O(n) from O(n log n). Accepted costs: every problem needs a large-input generator, timing on a normal machine is noisy, and the runner needs a second execution mode. Automated style nagging is noise and not what interviews reject people over. Grading on wall-clock would punish JVM warm-up and teach nothing. Thin attempt records would quietly cripple the scheduler, which takes this history as input.

rejected.alternative: Partial credit on correctness
rejected.why_it_lost: It would invent a number that means nothing and soften the only honest signal available.

rejected.alternative: Always handing over the failing case on failure
rejected.why_it_lost: It trains the opposite of reasoning about your own code without an oracle, which is why people grind hundreds of problems and still freeze.

rejected.alternative: Penalising use of the failing-case reveal
rejected.why_it_lost: Penalties on a self-imposed system only teach the user to game themselves.

rejected.alternative: Accepting the complexity self-report on its own
rejected.why_it_lost: Unverified, it would congratulate an O(n^2) solution claiming to be O(n), the single case most worth catching.

rejected.alternative: Automated style feedback
rejected.why_it_lost: Style nagging is noise and is not what interviews reject people over.

rejected.alternative: Grading on time or memory limits
rejected.why_it_lost: Grading on wall-clock would punish JVM warm-up and teach nothing.

nodes.soundbite: A submission simply passes or fails, the failing case is shown only when you ask and the ask is recorded, and your own complexity claim is checked by measuring how the code scales.

nodes.title: Grader/Runner split with language-neutral test cases
nodes.question: What an exercise is independent of language and domain, what a test specification looks like, what contract a runner adapter satisfies, and how a submission flows from editor to verdict - such that Java plus another language, SQL, front end, concepts, and warm-up reps all fit without redesign.
nodes.decision: Grader and Runner are separated: a Grader decides pass or fail, a Runner only executes, and both are polymorphic. An Exercise is the authored unit with prompt, domain, tags, difficulty, hint ladder, response spec and grading spec; Form (Rep or Challenge) is an attribute, not a separate type; Response is Choice, ShortAnswer, Program, Query, and later Component. Test cases and function signatures are language-neutral JSON data, with a language adapter generating the stub and harness per language, adopting LeetCode's serialisation convention for trees and lists. The Runner is a swappable execution boundary (local process now, container if hosted) that Graders never see behind. Attempt is the durable record including hint rungs, complexity claim, measured scaling and abandonment; Submission is one press of run. Complexity measurement is optional metadata via InputGenerator and ScalingProbe. Every row belonging to a person carries a user id with one user seeded and no authentication.
nodes.why: Separating what the user produces from how it is judged stops 'exercise' from secretly meaning 'thing that runs code': a concept question has a Grader and no Runner, and warm-up reps exist in every domain rather than as an algorithms-only special case. Test cases as data are authored once and run in every language ever added, which is the difference between pluggable languages being real and being aspirational. The accepted constraint is that exercises are restricted to JSON-representable inputs and outputs, which most of Blind 75 satisfies, and front end is stated plainly as the one place the JSON-test-case model does not extend - the abstraction only has to not foreclose it.

rejected.alternative: The obvious design where Exercise means 'thing that runs code'
rejected.why_it_lost: Concepts and warm-up reps become special cases bolted on the side.

rejected.alternative: Writing test cases as JUnit code
rejected.why_it_lost: Every new language would require re-authoring the entire problem set, making pluggable languages aspirational rather than real.

rejected.alternative: Inventing a serialisation convention for trees and linked lists
rejected.why_it_lost: LeetCode's existing convention ([1,2,3,null,4]) is adopted instead, since the captain will be reading their problem statements anyway.

nodes.soundbite: A Grader decides pass or fail and a Runner only executes, and test cases are language-neutral JSON authored once, so any language or non-code domain plugs in without redesign.

nodes.title: Two schedulers over one shared attempt record
nodes.question: How the app chooses what the captain practises next: whether selection is spaced repetition on a known algorithm, weakness targeting from past results, topic coverage, or a combination; what signal feeds it; whether standard spaced-repetition intervals survive a 40-minute problem; and how cold-start and graduation behave.
nodes.decision: Two schedulers run over one shared record. Reps get a standard spaced-repetition due-date queue, SM-2 with the algorithm kept swappable. Challenges get a priority score instead of due dates - time since last attempt, how badly the last attempt went, under-covered patterns, and a hard floor on minimum interval - and the highest scorer takes the daily slot. The per-attempt record is collapsed into a single 0-5 quality score (5 clean first pass, 3 passed with hints or failing-case reveal, 1 failed or abandoned); for reps, correct-or-not plus the warm-up confidence signal feeds the same scale. Time taken is excluded. Review debt is served before new problems, with a weekly cap on introductions. Nothing is deleted - three clean passes earn an interval of months, which is retirement not removal. An 'interview soon' mode is a re-weighted scoring function that favours broad recency and drops the minimum-interval floor, not a different app. Once SQL exercises exist, the daily rep set mixes domains in one queue, with domain as one more coverage dimension.
nodes.why: Spaced repetition assumes reviews are cheap; twenty due cards cost four minutes, but twenty due 30-40 minute challenges is a fortnight of work, and a scheduler that generates impossible debt gets ignored within a week. Scarcity is structural: roughly 90 challenge slots in three months against ~75 problems leaves barely room for one pass, let alone spaced review. Due dates ask what is owed; a priority score asks what is worth it, and only the second survives scarcity. Collapsing the attempt record to a 0-5 score maps directly onto SM-2 and keeps the scheduler from ossifying around today's exact recorded fields. The weekly cap prevents burning through ~75 problems in two months and arriving at breadth with no depth.

rejected.alternative: One scheduler serving both reps and challenges (due dates for challenges)
rejected.why_it_lost: The flashcard arithmetic breaks completely for a 30-40 minute challenge: twenty due challenges is a fortnight of work, and a scheduler that generates impossible debt gets ignored within a week.

rejected.alternative: FSRS for the rep queue
rejected.why_it_lost: Better on paper, but the difference over SM-2 is marginal at the scale of one user and ~400 reps.

rejected.alternative: Feeding raw per-attempt fields into either algorithm
rejected.why_it_lost: Collapsing to a single 0-5 quality score maps directly onto SM-2 and keeps the scheduler from ossifying around today's exact set of recorded fields.

rejected.alternative: Time taken as a scheduling signal
rejected.why_it_lost: It is noise: interruptions, thinking before typing, and typing fast on a misunderstood problem all corrupt it, adding variance without carrying information.

rejected.alternative: Unbounded introduction of new material
rejected.why_it_lost: The classic Anki failure: review debt piles up and the user quits; the cap also prevents burning through ~75 problems in two months with everything half-remembered.

rejected.alternative: Deleting problems passed cleanly three times
rejected.why_it_lost: A long interval of months is retirement, not removal; nothing is ever deleted.

rejected.alternative: A separate per-domain queue once SQL exercises exist
rejected.why_it_lost: The scheduler operates over exercises, and domain is one more coverage dimension alongside topic, not a reason for a second queue.

rejected.alternative: A different app for the final fortnight before interviews
rejected.why_it_lost: The objective change is a different scoring function that re-weights toward broad recency and drops the minimum-interval floor - cheap to build inside the same app.

nodes.soundbite: Reps come due on a spaced-repetition queue, and each day's challenge slot goes to whichever problem a priority score says is the best use of forty minutes.

nodes.title: Local Spring Boot web app on the existing banking-app stack
nodes.question: Where does swe-prep run and what is it built with: the shape (local web app, desktop app, CLI/TUI, or something else), where state lives, and the stack, weighed primarily against time-to-first-keystroke and secondarily against being a credible portfolio artifact.
nodes.decision: A local web app: Spring Boot 3.4.3 on Java 21 (Spring Web, Data JPA, Actuator, Lombok) with Postgres, a React + Vite front end, and Monaco as the code editor, reusing the Team-7-Banking-Application stack. It runs locally, autostarted via a systemd user unit, reached over the tailnet from other devices. Hosting is not built now but is protected by three choices: Postgres from the start, the runner behind an interface, and a user id modeled on every owned row with exactly one seeded user and no authentication.
nodes.why: Domain coverage decides the shape: grading front-end practice means rendering and asserting in a browser, which a terminal app can never do and a desktop app could only fake by embedding a browser. The friction weakness of a web app is answered by autostart on systemd, making time-to-first-keystroke one click. Reusing the banking-app stack removes learning cost and stack-selection risk, and a Spring Boot backend is itself portfolio evidence since entry-level Java postings screen for it. Postgres removes any database migration if hosted later. Modeling the user from day one makes adding auth later roughly a day's work, whereas an implicit single user makes it a refactor touching every table and query; building login now would also put a login screen between the captain and the daily drill.

rejected.alternative: A CLI/TUI
rejected.why_it_lost: It can never grade front-end practice, which requires rendering and asserting in a browser; the record notes it would genuinely have had the lowest friction, but the decision was made on domain coverage, not friction.

rejected.alternative: A desktop app
rejected.why_it_lost: It would have to embed a browser to fake front-end grading, adding a second platform later.

rejected.alternative: SQLite
rejected.why_it_lost: Its only real advantage was needing no service, which is worth little against Postgres already configured, and Postgres removes any migration if the app is ever hosted.

rejected.alternative: Building authentication now
rejected.why_it_lost: The captain has already built Spring Security once, so the login itself is not the cost; a login screen would add friction to the one thing whose purpose is removing friction, and modeling the user id without auth captures the expensive part.

rejected.alternative: Hosting now
rejected.why_it_lost: The captain does not need hosted access today; Tailscale already covers reaching it from a phone at zero cost, with the accepted limitation that the PC must be on.

nodes.soundbite: It runs as a local Spring Boot web app with Postgres and a React front end, autostarted so opening it is one click.

nodes.title: Two-tier daily session with a small required core
nodes.question: What one daily session looks like: how long it takes, how many exercises it contains, what happens on a wrong answer or when stuck, what "done for today" means, whether it is a fixed serving or open-ended, and whether partial completion counts - all under the tension that a hard algorithm problem can take 40 minutes while the daily serving must stay small.
nodes.decision: A session is three tiers and only the first is required: a warm-up of ~8 quick recall and recognition reps taking about 4 minutes, which alone completes the day; an optional main exercise of one full problem at roughly 30 minutes; and an uncapped open continuation afterward. Wrong warm-up answers are corrected immediately and re-queued in the same session; a stuck main exercise offers a user-chosen hint ladder (pattern name, approach, key insight, solution) with every rung recorded; the warm-up alone counts for the streak while an abandoned exercise is recorded as abandoned for the scheduler; and the session shape is domain-agnostic, with nothing allowed to assume the content is an algorithm problem.
nodes.why: The minimum session has to be small enough that it is never skipped, because bad days are the only days that matter and one skip usually ends the habit. The warm-up is not filler: pattern recognition is the highest-value-per-minute training for entry-level interviews, and the main exercises convert recognition into execution. Separating the streak (measures showing up) from the exercises (measure improving) keeps a self-imposed streak honest. Calibration with the captain confirmed the warm-up reads as genuinely valuable and four minutes is small enough for a bad day.

rejected.alternative: A 40-minute minimum daily session built around one full problem
rejected.why_it_lost: A 40-minute minimum is a session you skip when tired, and one skip usually ends the habit.

nodes.soundbite: A day is done after an eight-rep, four-minute warm-up, and the full problem and anything after it are optional.

nodes.title: Streak mechanics without invented currency
nodes.question: What actually generates the pull to open the app tomorrow, given that the captain is the only user and the author, knows any points are invented, and can edit the database - so self-imposed currency creates no obligation.
nodes.decision: Invented currency is cut entirely - no XP, no hearts, no lives, no leagues. Instead: every solved problem is committed to a private repo with private contributions shown on the profile, so the contribution graph is a real external record; the app shows an honest readiness picture (patterns covered, stale patterns, solved-cold counts) derived from the attempt records judging and scheduling already keep; a notification fires at a chosen time so the decision to practise is not made fresh each day; the streak is displayed as a true count of days practised, not spendable and nothing denominated in it; and a missed day may be repaired by a double session the next day, capped at roughly two per month. Hard rule: commit real artifacts only, never synthetic practice markers.
nodes.why: Any number the captain can print himself is a number he stops believing in around week two, and a fake number that goes up is actively misleading about whether he is getting hired. What the design can do is narrower and more honest: remove every excuse, make the record true rather than invented, and make breaking it cost something real. The contribution graph is external, permanent, and cannot be faked by the app; the readiness figures cost nothing to compute and are all true, creating pull because they are specific and honest about something the captain actually wants; habit research is consistent that the cue matters more than the motivation; and an all-or-nothing streak that breaks makes people quit outright rather than resume, which the capped repair prevents across one bad evening. The record also notes the lever that beats everything in the ticket - telling one person - cannot be built, and that if this design fails the answer is not more gamification.

rejected.alternative: Invented currency: XP, hearts, lives, leagues
rejected.why_it_lost: Any number the captain can print himself he stops believing in around week two, and a fake rising number is actively misleading about whether he is getting hired.

rejected.alternative: Publishing solutions to a public repo
rejected.why_it_lost: A public dump of Blind 75 solutions reads as interview grinding rather than building, and it would collide with the licensing question if statements ride along; nothing that mattered is lost since the witness function was never about anyone reading the solutions.

rejected.alternative: Synthetic 'practice happened' commit markers
rejected.why_it_lost: Auto-inflating a contribution graph is gaming, and the captain would know.

rejected.alternative: Financial stakes (Beeminder-style)
rejected.why_it_lost: They genuinely work, but wiring up money is real friction, and adding a punishment to an activity already being avoided is more likely to increase the avoidance; available later if nothing else lands.

nodes.soundbite: The streak sticks because everything shown is true - real commits, an honest readiness picture, a scheduled cue, and a repairable streak - and every invented number is cut.

nodes.title: Warm-up rep types, grading, and authoring
nodes.question: What a warm-up rep concretely is in each domain, which rep types exist, how each is answered and graded, where the reps come from, and how they relate to the main problem set.
nodes.decision: Five rep types: pattern identification, complexity of a snippet, fill in the missing line, predict the output, and spot the bug (added to the original sketch). Multiple choice by default, with predict-the-output as free text graded by exact match after normalisation. Every rep carries an explanation, shown immediately on a wrong answer, hidden by default on a correct one, always one keystroke away, with asking recorded as a signal. Nearly every rep is derived from a problem already being authored - five to six reps per problem, ~75 problems yielding roughly 400 reps, LLM-drafted and human-verified, with explanations generated in the same pass and verified alongside the rep. Derived reps unlock as problems are attempted; ~75 pattern-ID reps work cold on day one. The reference solution is the seed for everything, so there is one content pile, not two.
nodes.why: Reps train recognition and discrimination while production is what the Challenge exercises are for - a division of labour, not a compromise. Spot-the-bug is code review, which is genuinely the job, and coheres with the judging decision to make the captain reason about code without an oracle. Plausible distractors are the entire value of a rep in a four-minute daily budget. Explanations on wrong answers are the teaching moment, and recording that the captain asked why gives a free behavioural confidence signal without interrupting. Deriving reps from the problem set dissolves what would otherwise be a second content pile the size of the first, which is where the project most plausibly dies, and eight reps a day against a ~400-rep pool is comfortably sufficient since repetition is the point under spaced repetition.

rejected.alternative: Executing a typed line for fill-in-the-missing-line
rejected.why_it_lost: A Java compile takes a second or two and eight of those destroys the four-minute session; discrimination is the target anyway.

rejected.alternative: Free text for complexity answers
rejected.why_it_lost: The answer set is finite, so multiple choice grades exactly; free text would only mean normalising O(n^2) against O(n squared) for no benefit.

rejected.alternative: Buying the confidence signal by interrupting with a 'how hard was that?' prompt, as flashcard systems do
rejected.why_it_lost: Users learn to click through it; the same signal comes from behaviour that would happen anyway, and the scheduler can resurface the rep sooner without ever asking.

nodes.soundbite: A warm-up rep is one of five short recognition drills, mostly multiple choice, and nearly all of them are derived from problems the set already authors.

nodes.title: Assert no private content is committed
nodes.what: .github/workflows/ci.yml carries a step that fails the build on a policy breach rather than on a failing test.
nodes.why_interesting: Enforcing a rule in CI is a decision to stop trusting discipline. The rule is what someone was afraid of.

nodes.title: Grading is sealed over 4 permitted types
nodes.what: Grading permits exactly Grading.TestCases, Grading.AnswerKey, Grading.SelfCheck, Grading.ResultSet. The compiler rejects any implementation outside that set.
nodes.why_interesting: A sealed hierarchy is a closed enumeration the type system enforces. It is also one of the few things that can witness an absence claim, because the set is provably complete.

nodes.title: The record names docker; the build file does not declare it
nodes.statement: README.md refers to docker, but no build manifest in the tree declares a dependency on it.
nodes.why_it_matters: The stack a project says it uses and the stack it declares drift apart quietly, and the drift is what a reviewer finds first.
nodes.how_to_say_it: The README still mentions docker; the build no longer depends on it.

nodes.title: SelfCheckGrader.grade refuses where its siblings return
nodes.what: grade throws outright here, while 3 other implementations return a value.
nodes.why_interesting: The asymmetry is the design: someone decided this case must fail loudly rather than return something plausible. That choice is invisible unless you compare siblings.

findings: d-issue-10-c5182571856-divergence: The first sentence claims the tree does not carry the SQL exercise machinery as a whole, but the only tree evidence is a single grep showing 'order_items' absent, which establishes only that one table name is missing, not that the fixture database, runner, or other schemas are absent.

d-issue-2-c5181222288: 'It runs locally, autostarted via a systemd user unit, reached over the tailnet from other devices' asserts current runtime facts, but the cited evidence only records the decision to do so - no unit file or tailnet config is cited (and the pom shows 3.4.7 with starter-jdbc, not the 3.4.3/Data JPA/Lombok stack stated).

m-ci-guard-ci-yml-test-assert-no-private-content-is-committed: Sentence 'Enforcing a rule in CI is a decision to stop trusting discipline. The rule is what someone was afraid of.' asserts motive and fear; the cited step name establishes neither.

e-divergence-docker: Sentence 1 (and 3) claims 'no build manifest in the tree declares a dependency on it', but the only cited evidence is README.md, which shows docker is mentioned yet establishes nothing about what the build manifests declare.

m-refuses-backend-src-main-java-com-sweprep-backend-grader-selfcheckgrader-selfcheckgrader-grade-exercise-string: The first sentence claims '3 other implementations return a value', but the cited evidence shows only SelfCheckGrader throwing - no sibling implementations or their return behavior appear in the evidence.

checks.name: Each absence claim's citation actually witnesses absence
findings: fl-record-submissionrepository-countsforattempts-c6f6f0b5: The sentence 'No derivation drawn here reaches another: the closed symbol graph over this subject takes none of them to any of the others' is witnessed by nothing cited - every excerpt is a positive call site, SQL read, or derive method establishing the arrows that ARE drawn, and no cited span shows a reachability closure, negative search, or closed enumeration proving the branches cannot reach each other.

d-issue-2-c5181222288: The sentence 'exactly one seeded user and no authentication' (and 'Hosting is not built now') is only stated by the resolution comment, which is a decision, not a witness of the tree; the pom/package.json dependency lists at most show no security library, but nothing cited enumerates a seed migration, auth code, or deployment config, so the absences are asserted, not established.

e-divergence-docker: The sentence 'no build manifest in the tree declares a dependency on it' cites only README.md, which shows the docker mention but neither a negative search over manifests nor an enumeration of them, so the absence is unwitnessed.
